processing: Little is documented about how this tea is made. The name means tender green, which points to young leaf processed as an unoxidised green tea.
harvest_season: Not recorded for this tea; Sichuan tender greens are typically picked in early spring.
appearance_dry: Not well recorded; the name suggests young, fresh green leaf.
appearance_liquor: Typical of tender Sichuan greens: a clear, pale yellow-green.
appearance_wet: Typical of tender greens: soft, small, even green leaf.
taste_profile: No reliable tasting description exists for this tea; tender Sichuan greens generally taste fresh, lightly vegetal and sweet.

brewing.notes: A general method for tender green tea; adjust to the leaf in front of you.

vintage_note: Nothing specific is recorded about how this tea is sold. Green teas of its class are normally sold as the current spring harvest and are best within about a year.
description:
Wenjun Nenlü is a name listed for a green tea from Qionglai in Sichuan, but no source describing it as a product could be found. Nenlü simply means tender green, and Wenjun is the local name also carried by Qionglai's better documented Wenjun green tea.

Anything said about its leaf and cup here is what is typical of tender Sichuan greens, not a record of this tea.

If you come across it, brew it like any young spring green, with water well off the boil, and ask the seller for the picking date and who made it.
history: Little is documented about this tea: no clear record of when it was first made, by whom, or whether it remains in production.
